questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025, the Board of a licensed life insurance company must include a majority of:

opts.x: Executive directors with at least ten years of insurance industry experience.
Non-executive directors, with at least two independent directors.
Government-appointed directors representing NAICOM's supervisory interest.
Directors who are fellows of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria.

questions.answer: (B) Non-executive directors, with at least two independent directors.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 and the NAICOM Corporate Governance Code require that a majority of the Board of a licensed life insurer must be Non-Executive Directors (NEDs), with at least two of those NEDs meeting the definition of Independent Non-Executive Director (INED: no material financial relationship beyond Board fees; not formerly employed by the insurer; not connected to major shareholders). This majority NED requirement ensures that the Board provides independent oversight of management, a key governance safeguard against management-dominated Boards that have characterised some historical insurer failures.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Executive directors, while they may bring operational expertise, must be a minority on the Board under NIIRA 2025. An executive-dominated Board cannot provide the independent oversight the governance framework requires.
(C) NAICOM does not appoint directors to regulated insurers' Boards; this would constitute regulatory capture and conflict of interest. NAICOM supervises the insurer but does not sit on its Board.
(D) FCIIN qualification is a professional credential, respected but not a NIIRA 2025 Board composition requirement.

questions.stem: In the Three Lines of Defence model mandated by NIIRA 2025, the Internal Audit function is the:

opts.x: First line, which manages day-to-day operational risks.
Second line, which designs the risk framework and monitors compliance.
Third line, which provides independent assurance to the Board on the effectiveness of the first two lines.
Fourth line, which provides assurance to NAICOM on behalf of all licensed insurers.

questions.answer: (C) Third line, which provides independent assurance to the Board on the effectiveness of the first and second lines.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

The Three Lines of Defence model assigns:
• First Line: Business functions (underwriting, claims, sales, investments) that own and manage risk as they take it on.
• Second Line: Risk management, compliance, and actuarial functions that provide oversight and challenge to the first line.
• Third Line: Internal Audit, which provides independent assurance to the Board that BOTH the first and second lines are operating effectively. Internal Audit's independence from management (it reports to the Board's Audit Committee) is what gives its assurance value; it is not subject to the management pressures that can compromise the first and second lines.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The first line is the business operations, not Internal Audit.
(B) The second line is the risk and compliance functions, not Internal Audit.
(D) There is no 'fourth line' in the standard Three Lines of Defence model. NAICOM performs supervisory oversight externally but is not part of the internal governance structure.

questions.stem: The Delegation of Authority document in a life insurance company:

opts.x: Specifies the minimum qualifications required for each senior management position.
Maps the chain of financial and operational approval authority from the Board down through management to individual managers.
Lists the insurance products that have received NAICOM product approval.
Sets out the annual performance targets agreed between the Board and the MD/CEO.

questions.answer: (B) Maps the chain of financial and operational approval authority from the Board down through management to individual managers.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The Delegation of Authority (DoA) document is a governance instrument that specifies: what financial commitments can be approved at each management level (a claims assessor can approve payments up to ₦5m; the Head of Claims up to ₦50m; the MD/CEO up to ₦500m; the Board above that); what operational decisions require the relevant functional head's sign-off; and what decisions cannot be made below Board level under any circumstances. The DoA prevents unauthorised commitments, creates accountability at each management level, and provides the audit trail that the Board and NAICOM need to verify that governance is operating as designed.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Staff qualification requirements are set out in the insurer's HR policy and NIIRA 2025 fit-and-proper requirements, not the DoA.
(C) The NAICOM product approval schedule is a regulatory compliance document, separate from the DoA.
(D) MD/CEO performance targets are set in the employment contract and the Board's performance scorecard, not the DoA.

questions.stem: The Statutory Actuary's primary regulatory obligation under NIIRA 2025 is to:

opts.x: Manage the insurer's investment portfolio within the Board-approved Investment Policy Statement.
Certify the annual actuarial investigation, including the adequacy of the insurer's technical provisions, with a direct reporting line to the Board.
Review and approve each new product filing before it is submitted to NAICOM.
Monitor the insurer's compliance with the Pension Reform Act 2014 and PenCom guidelines.

questions.answer: (B) Certify the annual actuarial investigation, including the adequacy of the insurer's technical provisions, with a direct reporting line to the Board.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The Statutory Actuary's most fundamental obligation under NIIRA 2025 is the annual actuarial valuation and certification, calculating and certifying that the insurer's technical provisions (policy reserves, outstanding claims provisions, and other actuarial liabilities) are adequate to meet the insurer's policy obligations. The Statutory Actuary reports the results of this investigation to the Board and files the actuarial certificate with NAICOM as part of the annual regulatory return. The direct reporting line to the Board (not only to management) is the critical governance feature, it enables the Statutory Actuary to escalate material concerns directly to the Board if management does not address them.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Investment portfolio management is the CIO's responsibility, governed by the ALCO, not the Statutory Actuary's primary function (though the Actuary advises on ALM requirements).
(C) Product filing review is part of the Statutory Actuary's work but is not the primary regulatory obligation, certification of the annual valuation is.
(D) PRA 2014/PenCom compliance monitoring is an HR and legal function, not the Statutory Actuary's mandate.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the Board's Risk Committee in a Nigerian life insurer is to:

opts.x: Approve the payment of claims above a defined monetary threshold.
Review and approve the Risk Appetite Statement; oversee the ERM framework; and monitor the insurer's emerging risks.
Approve all new reinsurance treaties and review the cedant's cession programme annually.
Oversee the integrity of the financial statements and manage the relationship with the external auditor.

questions.answer: (B) Review and approve the Risk Appetite Statement; oversee the ERM framework; and monitor the insurer's emerging risks.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The Board's Risk Committee is the delegated governance body responsible for NIIRA 2025's ERM requirements at the Board level. Its primary responsibilities include: reviewing the Risk Appetite Statement and recommending it to the full Board for approval; overseeing the design and effectiveness of the ERM framework (including the Three Lines of Defence); reviewing the ORSA before NAICOM submission; monitoring KRIs and the risk register; and receiving the Statutory Actuary's and CRO's reports on material risks.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Claims approval above a threshold is an executive (Head of Claims or MD/CEO) authority, not a Board committee function.
(C) Reinsurance treaty approval is a management function; the Board Risk Committee may receive a report on the reinsurance programme but does not typically approve individual treaties.
(D) Financial statement integrity and external auditor management are the Board Audit Committee's responsibilities, not the Risk Committee's.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer with 180 employees, ₦45bn in gross written premium, and distribution through agents, bancassurance, and a digital channel is undertaking an organisational restructuring to comply with NIIRA 2025. Currently, the CRO reports to the CFO; the Compliance function is combined with Legal under a single manager; and the Internal Audit function reports to the MD/CEO.
(a) Identify the three specific governance deficiencies in the current structure and explain why each is non-compliant with NIIRA 2025 or best-practice governance standards.
(b) Describe the corrected reporting structure for the CRO, Compliance, and Internal Audit functions, explaining the governance rationale for each change.
(c) Describe the composition of the Board’s Risk Committee and Audit Committee required for this insurer under NIIRA 2025.
(d) Explain the key changes to the insurer’s Delegation of Authority document that would be required to reflect the restructured governance arrangements.

model.h: Part (a): Three Governance Deficiencies

rows: The CRO's independence requires a direct reporting line to the Board or the Board Risk Committee, not to a fellow ExCo member who may be subject to the same management pressures and business targets as the risks the CRO is supposed to challenge. If the CRO reports to the CFO, the CFO can suppress or dilute the CRO's risk escalations before they reach the Board, eliminating the second line's independence. NIIRA 2025 requires the CRO to have unfettered access to the Board.
Compliance combined with Legal under a single manager

The Compliance function's role is to provide independent oversight of regulatory compliance, challenging business decisions that create regulatory risk. The Legal function's role is to protect the insurer's legal interests, which may sometimes include finding ways to limit regulatory exposure rather than proactively report it. Combining the two creates an inherent tension: a single manager responsible for both regulatory compliance (which may require escalating concerns to NAICOM) and legal risk management (which may counsel against escalation) will face irreconcilable conflicts. NIIRA 2025's market conduct framework requires the Compliance function to have unambiguous independence.

Internal Audit must report to the Board Audit Committee, not to the MD/CEO, to maintain its independence. If Internal Audit reports to the MD/CEO, the CEO can influence the scope of Internal Audit work, delay or suppress unfavourable findings, and limit Internal Audit's access to areas of the business that might embarrass management. The Third Line of Defence's assurance value depends entirely on its independence from the management it is assessing.

model.h: Part (b): Corrected Reporting Structure

CRO: The CRO must report directly to the MD/CEO for operational coordination, but must have an independent reporting line (including the right to report without management present) to the Board Risk Committee. The Board Risk Committee Chair should have a regular private meeting with the CRO without management present, at least quarterly.

Compliance: The Head of Compliance must report directly to the MD/CEO (for operational purposes) but with a guaranteed independent line to the Board Audit Committee. Compliance and Legal should be separated into distinct functions; each with their own head. The Head of Compliance should have the explicit right to report directly to NAICOM if management does not adequately address a material compliance breach.

Internal Audit: The Head of Internal Audit must report functionally to the Board Audit Committee, with the Audit Committee approving the Head of Internal Audit's appointment, annual audit plan, and remuneration. The Head of Internal Audit should have the right to access any area of the business, any records, and any member of staff. The MD/CEO receives administrative (day-to-day operational) support from Internal Audit but has no authority over the Audit function's scope, findings, or reporting.
Part (c): Board Risk Committee and Audit Committee Composition

Board Risk Committee (BRC):
• Minimum three members, all Non-Executive Directors
• Chair: An INED with risk management, actuarial, or financial risk expertise
• Composition: At least one INED with direct insurance or financial services risk experience
• Statutory Actuary and CRO attend as permanent invitees (non-members)
• Frequency: Minimum quarterly meetings; additional meetings as required by the ORSA calendar

Board Audit Committee (BAC):
• Minimum three members, all Non-Executive Directors
• Chair: An INED with financial reporting or audit expertise
• At least one member should have specific IFRS accounting knowledge (IFRS 17 from the adoption date)
• Head of Internal Audit and Head of Compliance attend as permanent invitees
• External auditors attend for the audit planning meeting and the year-end audit findings presentation
• The BAC Chair should meet privately with Internal Audit and the external auditors without management present at least annually
Part (d): DoA Changes Required

The restructured governance arrangements require the following DoA updates:

1. CRO escalation authority: The DoA must document the CRO's authority to escalate any risk concern directly to the Board Risk Committee, bypassing the MD/CEO if necessary, without management approval. This right cannot be subject to management veto.

2. Compliance escalation authority: The Compliance function's authority to: (a) put a 'compliance hold' on any new business activity or product launch pending regulatory review; and (b) report directly to NAICOM in the event of a material NIIRA 2025 breach that management has not addressed within a prescribed period.

3. Internal Audit access rights: The DoA must document Internal Audit's unrestricted right to access all business areas, all records, all systems, and all staff, with no management approval required for an Internal Audit review.

4. Separation of Compliance and Legal approval authorities: With Compliance and Legal now separate functions, the DoA must specify which decisions require Compliance sign-off (market conduct issues; regulatory filings; product marketing approval) and which require Legal sign-off (contract execution; litigation management; regulatory proceedings), replacing the combined single-manager approval with dual-function approval where both dimensions are relevant.

questions.stem:
A newly licensed Nigerian life insurer is in its first year of operation with 45 employees, ₦8bn in initial capital, and a plan to distribute through agents and a bancassurance partnership.
(a) Design the organisational structure for this start-up insurer, specifying which functions should be combined, which must remain independent, and the reporting lines to the MD/CEO.
(b) Identify the four most critical integration mechanisms this insurer must establish from day one, explaining why each is critical at the start-up stage.
(c) Describe the minimum governance documents that must be in place before NAICOM will approve the company’s operational commencement.
(d) Explain at what growth stage the start-up should begin separating combined functions into dedicated departments, and which separations should happen first.

model.h: Part (a): Start-Up Organisational Structure (45 Employees)

At 45 employees, a full separated-function structure (separate departments for each governance function) is neither financially feasible nor operationally necessary. The structure should be:

Board level: MD/CEO; Board (minimum 5 directors: majority NEDs, at least 2 INEDs); Board Risk Committee; Board Audit Committee.

ExCo level (4–5 senior leaders reporting to MD/CEO):
1. Chief Technical Officer (combined Underwriting + Claims + Actuarial support): One senior technical leader overseeing all product technical functions.
2. CFO (Finance + Investment): Manages the financial reporting; works with the ALCO.
3. Chief Distribution Officer (Sales + Bancassurance + Agency Management): Single distribution function.
4. Head of Operations (IT/PAS + HR + Administration): Operational infrastructure.

Functions that must remain independent (even at start-up scale):
1. Internal Audit: Must report to the Board Audit Committee, not to the MD/CEO. At this scale, Internal Audit may be a single outsourced function (a co-sourced arrangement with a professional services firm), but cannot be subordinated to management.
2. Compliance: Cannot be merged into Legal. The Compliance officer must have a direct Board access channel even if they administratively report to the MD/CEO.
3. Statutory Actuary: Must be a qualified actuary with direct access to the Board, may be part-time or contracted externally, but cannot be subordinated to the CFO.

Functions that can be combined at start-up:
• Underwriting + Claims (under the CTO)
• Finance + Investment (under the CFO)
• HR + IT + Administration (under Head of Operations)
Part (b): Four Most Critical Integration Mechanisms from Day One

1. ExCo weekly meeting: The four-person ExCo must meet weekly to share information across functions, the most basic integration mechanism. A start-up where the CTO, CFO, and CDO operate in separate information silos will have its financial model, distribution strategy, and technical underwriting become misaligned within months.

2. Unified CRM-PAS data flow: From day one, all customer data must flow between the distribution system (CRM) and the policy record system (PAS) without manual intervention. At a start-up with 45 employees, manual data entry between systems is both error-prone and time-consuming; the data integration must be built at inception, not retrofitted.

3. Claims-Underwriting feedback loop: A weekly briefing between the underwriting officer and the claims officer ensures that early claims experience (particularly on the first 200–300 policies written) is immediately fed back to the underwriting criteria, catching systematic risk selection errors before they accumulate into a portfolio problem.

4. Finance-Actuarial monthly meeting: The CFO and the Statutory Actuary must meet monthly (minimum) to: reconcile financial accounting data with actuarial reserve calculations; review the premium collection against pricing assumptions; and produce the monthly management accounts, integrating the actuarial view of the business with the accounting view.
Part (c): Minimum Governance Documents Before NAICOM Approval

NAICOM requires the following governance documents before approving operational commencement:

1. Board-approved Board Charter, specifying the Board's composition requirements, committee structure, and decision-making authorities.
2. Delegation of Authority document, signed by the Board.
3. Risk Appetite Statement, approved by the Board.
4. Investment Policy Statement (IPS), approved by the Board.
5. Compliance Policy and AML Policy, approved by the Board.
6. Fit and Proper applications for all Board members and key function holders, approved by NAICOM.
7. Statutory Actuary certificate of appointment, filed with NAICOM.
8. Business Plan (3-year), approved by the Board and filed with NAICOM.
9. NAICOM product approval certificates for all products to be offered at launch.
10. Corporate agency agreement for the bancassurance partnership, filed with NAICOM.
Part (d): Growth-Stage Function Separation Triggers

Function separations should be triggered by volume and compliance complexity, not by a specific employee count. The following growth triggers should prompt separation:

First separation (approximately year 2–3, GWP ₦15–₦20bn): Separate Underwriting from Claims, create a dedicated Head of Claims. Reason: As claim volumes grow, the conflict of interest in having the same leader oversee both risk acceptance and claims settlement becomes practically significant (and technically a governance concern under NIIRA 2025's market conduct framework).

Second separation (approximately year 3–4, GWP ₦25–₦30bn): Separate Finance from Investment, create a dedicated CIO or Head of Investments reporting to the ALCO. Reason: As the investment portfolio grows toward ₦5bn+, the complexity of ALM management exceeds the generalist CFO's bandwidth. Also: the ALCO governance requirement under NIIRA 2025 functions most effectively with a dedicated investment specialist.

Third separation (approximately year 4–5, GWP ₦40bn+): Create a dedicated HR function, separate from Operations. Reason: As the employee base approaches 150+, talent management, training compliance (CIIN qualification tracking), performance management, and compensation design become sufficiently complex to require dedicated HR expertise.

questions.stem:
The Underwriting and Claims departments of a Nigerian life insurer are in persistent conflict: the Underwriting Head believes Claims is settling too many contested claims without adequate investigation; the Claims Head believes Underwriting is accepting risks that should be declined. Both heads report to the same ExCo member.
(a) Diagnose the organisational and management failure that has allowed this conflict to persist.
(b) Design the integration mechanisms that should connect the Underwriting and Claims functions in a well-structured life insurer.
(c) Describe the role of the Statutory Actuary in resolving this conflict by providing objective mortality experience data.
(d) Explain how the Board’s Risk Committee should be informed of and involved in managing this operational dispute.

model.h: Part (a): Organisational and Management Failure Diagnosis

The persistent conflict between Underwriting and Claims is not primarily a personality conflict; it is a governance and information failure:

1. Absence of shared performance metrics: Underwriting is measured on premium income written and risk quality of accepted business; Claims is measured on settlement speed and claimant satisfaction. These metrics create divergent incentives: Underwriting is incentivised to accept marginal risks to grow the book; Claims is incentivised to settle contested claims quickly to meet service standards. Neither function has a metric that requires them to work together toward the shared outcome of sustainable portfolio profitability.

2. Absence of systematic data sharing: The conflict is partly an information asymmetry problem. Underwriting makes acceptance decisions based on proposal form data and medical evidence; Claims sees the outcome of those decisions years later. Without a structured mechanism for Claims to feed mortality experience data back to Underwriting, the Underwriting function lacks the evidence to calibrate its risk assessment criteria.

3. Escalation failure: The ExCo member responsible for both functions has not resolved the conflict, suggesting either that they lack the technical authority (the dispute requires actuarial evidence to resolve) or that they have avoided making a decision that will make one of their direct reports unhappy. The conflict requires escalation to a level with both the authority and the analytical capability to resolve it.
Part (b): Integration Mechanisms Between Underwriting and Claims

1. Monthly Technical Review Committee: A structured meeting chaired by the CTO (or equivalent) with the Heads of Underwriting and Claims, reviewing: the month's new claims for any systematic patterns (a cluster of claims from the same agent's book may indicate underwriting mis-selection; a high decline rate on a specific product may indicate policy wording issues); the claims experience by product type and vintage year compared to pricing assumptions; and any new patterns that require immediate underwriting response.

2. Claims-back analysis protocol: For every declined or contested claim above ₦50m, a formal claims-back analysis is conducted, reviewing the original underwriting decision in the context of the claim outcome. Did the underwriting decision miss a risk indicator that in retrospect was visible? If so, the underwriting criteria are updated. This creates a continuous feedback loop that improves underwriting quality over time.

3. Shared KPI: Introduce a joint Underwriting-Claims KPI: the loss ratio by underwriting cohort (policies accepted in the same year by the same underwriter). This creates a shared accountability for the portfolio's performance: Underwriting is not just measured on premium volume written but on the claims outcome of the risks they accepted.

4. Joint SIU referral protocol: Claims and Underwriting jointly agree the criteria for SIU referral, ensuring that Claims has the Underwriting team's technical analysis of risk acceptance history when assessing potentially fraudulent claims, and that Underwriting is notified of SIU investigation outcomes.
Part (c): Role of the Statutory Actuary

The Statutory Actuary can resolve the technical dispute between Underwriting and Claims by providing objective, actuarially grounded mortality experience data:

1. Annual mortality experience investigation: The Statutory Actuary conducts a formal analysis of actual vs expected mortality by product type, by underwriting year, and by underwriting decision category (standard; rated; exclusion). This analysis objectively answers the question: 'Is the Claims team settling more claims than the pricing assumption predicted?' If actual mortality is 110% of the EFU table assumptions, this confirms that either pricing is inadequate or underwriting is accepting too many substandard risks, evidence that Underwriting should tighten its criteria.

2. Lapse and claims correlation analysis: The Statutory Actuary's analysis can also address the Claims team's concern about excessive declined-then-contested claims, by analysing whether contested claims are more prevalent in specific underwriting cohorts, which would suggest that specific underwriting decisions (particular agents, particular products, particular medical evidence standards) are producing adverse claims selection.

3. Presentation to the ExCo and Board Risk Committee: The Statutory Actuary presents the experience investigation findings to the ExCo, providing objective, actuarially certified evidence that takes the dispute out of the realm of subjective perception and into quantified professional analysis. This gives the MD/CEO the technical authority to make decisions on underwriting criteria and claims settlement standards that are defensible to both departments.
Part (d): Board Risk Committee Involvement

When an operational dispute between two functions persists at ExCo level and is not resolved within a reasonable period (say, three months from the first formal escalation), it should be escalated to the Board Risk Committee as an operational risk matter:

1. Escalation trigger: The CRO (who monitors operational risks) identifies the Underwriting-Claims conflict as an operational risk, the lack of coordination between the two functions creates risk of both adverse selection (if Underwriting systematically ignores Claims feedback) and poor claims outcomes (if Claims systematically over-settles without adequate investigation). The CRO raises this in the quarterly Board Risk Committee report.

2. Board Risk Committee action: The BRC does not resolve the operational dispute itself; that is management's responsibility. The BRC: directs management to present a resolution plan within 30 days; requests the Statutory Actuary's mortality experience report as background; and sets a deadline for the introduction of the shared KPI and monthly Technical Review Committee mechanisms.

3. Progress monitoring: The BRC includes the Underwriting-Claims integration progress on its quarterly monitoring agenda until the mechanisms are confirmed to be operational, confirming that the governance failure has been addressed.

questions.stem: NIIRA 2025’s governance requirements for Nigerian life insurers (Board composition, three lines of defence, Statutory Actuary mandate, Board committees) represent a significant strengthening of the regulatory framework for insurance governance. Critically evaluate whether these requirements are sufficient to produce genuinely well-governed Nigerian life insurers, or whether structural compliance can coexist with substantive governance failure. In your answer, discuss: the distinction between formal compliance with governance requirements and genuine governance effectiveness; the specific conditions under which the three lines of defence model fails in practice; the role of Board culture and director independence in determining whether the formal governance structure delivers real oversight; and the additional measures (supervisory, cultural, or market-driven) that would need to accompany the NIIRA 2025 requirements to produce consistently high-quality insurance governance in Nigeria.

model.h: Thesis

NIIRA 2025's governance requirements are a necessary and significant improvement over the pre-2025 framework. They are not sufficient. The history of corporate governance failures globally (including in markets with far more sophisticated regulatory frameworks than Nigeria's) demonstrates consistently that formal governance compliance can coexist with substantive governance failure. The determining variable is not the sophistication of the governance architecture but the quality, independence, and courage of the people who operate within it.
Formal Compliance vs Genuine Governance Effectiveness

Formal compliance with NIIRA 2025's governance requirements means:
• The Board has a majority of NEDs, including at least two INEDs, but the INEDs were recommended by the controlling shareholder and feel a sense of loyalty that prevents genuine challenge.
• The Board Risk Committee meets quarterly and receives the CRO's risk report, but the Committee chairman does not understand actuarial risk or has not read the ORSA before the meeting.
• The Statutory Actuary certifies the technical provisions, but is a part-time consultant who relies on the CFO's data inputs and does not have independent access to the PAS to verify them.
• Internal Audit reports to the Board Audit Committee, but the Internal Audit function has two staff members and a budget of ₦15m per year for an insurer with ₦45bn GWP.

Each of these scenarios is technically compliant with NIIRA 2025's structural requirements. None of them produces genuine governance effectiveness.
Conditions Under Which the Three Lines of Defence Model Fails

The model fails when:
1. The first line has no risk culture: Business managers who treat every risk control as an obstacle to closing a sale will find ways around the controls, creating documentation that looks compliant while the underlying behaviour is unchanged.
2. The second line lacks authority: A CRO who fears that raising a concern will result in being marginalised (or eventually exited) will self-censor the risk escalation. A Compliance officer whose access to the MD/CEO is mediated by a CFO who is also the subject of some compliance concerns cannot provide independent oversight.
3. The third line is under-resourced: An Internal Audit function with two auditors cannot effectively audit three distribution channels, a bancassurance partnership, a digital platform, and all of the operational functions of a 180-employee insurer in any given year. Adequate resources are a prerequisite for effective third-line assurance.
4. The second and third lines are not independent of each other: If the Head of Compliance reports to the CFO and the Head of Internal Audit also has management reporting to the CFO, both oversight functions are compromised by the same management influence.
Board Culture and Director Independence

The most powerful governance variable is the culture of the Board itself, specifically, whether independent directors exercise genuine independent judgement or whether they treat their role as a prestigious appointment that requires deference to management.

Genuine Board independence requires:
1. Intellectual independence: INEDs who have the technical knowledge to understand what management is telling them, and the knowledge to know when they are not being told everything they should be.
2. Psychological independence: INEDs who are not socially or financially dependent on the insurer or its controlling shareholder, and who will therefore ask uncomfortable questions even when the MD/CEO is visibly irritated.
3. Access to information: INEDs who receive information directly from the CRO, the Statutory Actuary, and Internal Audit, not filtered through management. Private meetings between the Board Risk Committee and the CRO (without management present) are the most important governance mechanism that costs nothing to implement.

NIIRA 2025's INED definition (no financial relationship beyond Board fees; not formerly employed) addresses the structural aspects of independence. It cannot mandate the intellectual courage that genuine independence requires.
Additional Measures Required

1. NAICOM supervisory effectiveness: A governance framework is only as effective as the regulator's ability to identify when it is failing. NAICOM's market conduct inspection programme must evolve from checking governance documentation to assessing governance quality, reviewing the minutes of Board Risk Committee meetings for evidence of genuine challenge; interviewing directors independently of management; and assessing whether the CRO and Internal Audit function have the resource and access their mandate requires.

2. Director accountability: Where NAICOM identifies that a director participated in a governance failure (approved a decision they should have challenged; failed to ask for information they should have requested), there must be personal accountability consequences, not just corporate sanctions on the insurer. Personal accountability creates the incentive for genuine engagement.

3. Insurance governance code: The NIA or NAICOM should publish a best-practice insurance governance code (beyond the minimum NIIRA 2025 requirements), providing a framework against which self-assessed compliance can be compared by investors, rating agencies, and large corporate clients. Public transparency creates competitive incentive for governance quality improvement beyond the regulatory minimum.

questions.stem: ‘The organisational structure of a life insurance company is not a neutral administrative arrangement. It determines who hears bad news first; who has the authority to act on it; who is incentivised to suppress it; and whether the Board receives the information it needs to govern effectively. In the Nigerian insurance market, the most common cause of insurer distress is not bad luck or bad markets; it is structural governance failure: under-resourced second-line functions, inaccessible audit functions, and ExCo cultures that treat risk escalation as disloyalty.’ Critically evaluate this proposition, drawing on the governance principles in this chapter and on specific examples of organisational design failures and their consequences for Nigerian life insurers.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition identifies an underappreciated truth about Nigerian insurance market failures; that most insolvencies and distress events in the sector's history were preceded by identifiable governance failures that a well-structured organisation would have detected and addressed before they became existential. Structure is not destiny, but structure determines the probability of detecting and responding to bad news.
How Organisational Structure Determines Information Flow

Who hears bad news first:
In a poorly structured organisation, bad news travels up the hierarchy only as fast as management allows it. A CRO who reports to the CFO, whose compensation depends on the organisation's reported performance, may, consciously or unconsciously, soften the risk escalation to avoid creating a problem for the CFO. The Board hears about the deteriorating loss ratio six months after it became apparent, when the Statutory Actuary's annual valuation finally forces the issue.

In a well-structured organisation, bad news triggers automated alerts (the PAS dashboard shows the 60-day claims breach before any human decides whether to escalate); the CRO has a standing agenda item at the Board Risk Committee to present risk developments regardless of management's preferred narrative; and the Statutory Actuary certifies to the Board that the reserves are adequate, and refuses to certify if they are not.

Who has the authority to act:
The DoA document, the unglamorous infrastructure of governance, determines whether a senior claims assessor who identifies a systematic fraud pattern can immediately place a hold on the related claims, or whether they must navigate three layers of management approval before any action is taken. Fraud typically metastasises during management approval cycles.
Who Is Incentivised to Suppress Bad News

This is the most important governance design question. Every organisational structure creates incentives, some inadvertent, some structural:

1. Management performance incentives: An MD/CEO whose bonus is linked to annual GWP growth is incentivised to prioritise revenue over risk quality. An underwriting team whose targets are set in new business premium, without adjustment for the quality of the risk, is incentivised to accept marginal risks.

2. The 'shoot the messenger' culture: In organisations where raising a risk concern is perceived as obstructionism or disloyalty, risk escalation is suppressed. The claims officer who observes a systematic fraud pattern in a specific agency unit but knows that the agency unit belongs to the MD's nephew (and has seen what happened to the last person who raised a sensitive issue) will not escalate.

3. Governance design response: Commission clawback; persistency-linked bonus; CRO remuneration linked to risk quality metrics; explicit whistleblower protection in the employee handbook; and the Board's demonstrated willingness to act on escalated concerns; all of these structural elements determine whether the suppression incentive is overcome.
Evidence from Nigerian Insurance Market History

The pattern in Nigerian life insurer distress cases has been remarkably consistent:
1. Reserves inadequately calculated and certified; the Statutory Actuary function was either absent, insufficiently resourced, or compromised by management pressure.
2. Investment of life fund assets in related-party vehicles, no ALCO independence; no investment governance; no second-line challenge.
3. Premium misappropriation by agents or corporate intermediaries, no Premium Trust Account enforcement; no daily reconciliation; no independent audit of the premium collection process.
4. Management fraud discovered years after it began: Internal Audit either non-existent or reporting to the same management responsible for the fraud.

None of these failures required exceptionally bad luck or an unexpectedly bad market. Each was enabled by a governance structure that concentrated information and authority in the wrong hands, eliminated the independent challenge functions, and ensured that the Board heard bad news only when it was too late to address it.
Structural Change vs Cultural Change

The proposition's strongest claim is that structural failures cause distress, not bad luck or bad markets. This is broadly correct. But structure and culture interact: a well-designed governance structure in an organisation with a fundamentally corrupt or dishonest leadership team will be circumvented. NIIRA 2025's structural requirements create the governance architecture; leadership quality and integrity determine whether that architecture functions as intended.

The most durable solution is both structural (the governance reforms NIIRA 2025 mandates) and cultural (the leadership behaviours, incentive designs, and accountability mechanisms that make the formal structure work in practice). The insurer that understands this duality (that compliance with NIIRA 2025 is the floor, not the ceiling, of governance quality) will not merely avoid regulatory sanction. It will build an organisation that is more honest, more stable, and more commercially successful over the long term than one that treats governance as a compliance exercise.
